title: The Repeating Hand, narrated
lede: One carved shape, pressed again and again into cloth. A king from the Indus Valley wears a cloak that might have been printed, and nobody has proved it. This tour follows the evidence, and says exactly how much we know.

steps.title: A king in a patterned cloak
steps.text: About four thousand years ago, a king in the Indus Valley was carved in soapstone, wearing a cloak of three-leaf patterns. Was that cloth printed with a carved block? Nobody knows. This site follows the evidence.

steps.title: An open-data history
steps.text: It is an open-data history of block printing, the oldest way to copy a pattern. Every claim carries its source, and every quote is checked.

steps.title: Meet the Priest-King
steps.text: A three-D model of his soapstone bust, built from museum photographs. Drag to turn it. It is an interpretation, not a scan.

steps.title: What the sculpture shows
steps.text: Tap the dots to see what survives: the headband, the spiral ear, the beard, and the cloak of trefoils, each with a museum quote.

steps.title: Stone, or printed cloth?
steps.text: Now switch the stone to printed cloth. It is an illustration of the hypothesis, madder red on cotton. It is not evidence, and it says so.

steps.title: The honest part
steps.text: Every claim is sorted: evidenced, reported, not found, or imagined. No printing block from Mohenjo-daro appears in our sources, so that row says not found.

steps.title: How a block print is made
steps.text: How is a block print made? Carve a block, print a mordant or a resist, dye the cloth, then wash. The steps come from museum records.

steps.title: From cotton to calico
steps.text: Then scroll through the history: from the first cotton at Mehrgarh, to carved blocks in Egypt, Indian cottons found in Cairo, and the calico that changed Europe.

steps.title: When and where
steps.text: Every stop appears by region and date. Drag the slider, and whatever had not yet happened disappears.

steps.title: The blue thread
steps.text: Printed cloth is usually two colors: madder red and indigo blue. Cards from our indigo study show where the two stories meet.

steps.title: Claims that fail
steps.text: Some popular claims do not hold up. Does the shawl prove Indus printing? Not shown. See which fail the sources, and why.

steps.title: Every source, audited
steps.text: Every picture is rights-cleared, and the audit counts each claim as confirmed, pending or derived, so you can see what is solid and what is still a lead.

steps.title: Find your way
steps.text: Use the arrows to jump between sections or step through the timeline. The menu lists everything, and the sun and moon switch the theme.

steps.title: Free and open source
steps.text: The Repeating Hand is free and open source. The code, the data and the three-D model live in a public GitHub repo. Fork it, reuse it, and tell a different history.
